title: Nearing Grace
full_review:
Its spiritual sounding title notwithstanding, "Nearing Grace" (Whitewater) is not a religious film, though its young protagonist does experience a sort of secular conversion.

Set in 1979, the modest and melancholy coming-of-age drama revolves around Henry (Gregory Smith), an 18-year-old trying to cope after the recent death of his mother. His despairing father, Shep (David Morse), has quit his teaching job and taken up riding a motorcycle and numbing the pain with booze, while older brother Blair (David Moscow) shows up from time to time on their doorstep when he's not off with his girlfriend experimenting with mind-altering drugs.

On one level, the title refers to the object of Henry's lust, Grace (Jordana Brewster), a sexually aggressive high school seductress with whom he sleeps, much to the heartbreak of soul mate Merna (Ashley Johnson), who hopes to be more than friends.

On another level, it alludes to Henry's slow journey from anger and cynicism to seeing the beauty of things -- regardless of the pain -- with new eyes.

Director Rick Rosenthal's adaptation of Scott Sommer's novel touches on themes of love, loss and desire, and, despite the amorality of its characters in navigating their brokenness and grief, ultimately endorses a deeper appreciation of life and others.

The film contains sexual situations, teen smoking and drinking, drug content, an attempted suicide, rear nudity, a vulgar gesture, an irreligious dispersal of ashes, as well as rough, crude and sexually blunt language, and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
